summary:
Centinela is a web-based health console that helps astronauts on long-duration missions monitor, understand and act on their own health. On a mission to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 44 minutes round trip, so crews must catch health problems themselves.

Astronauts log indicators by keyboard and clicks, such as blood pressure, glucose in mg/dL, sleep, mood and symptoms. They can also measure their heart rate with the phone’s camera and flash. Simulated wearable sensors add oxygen saturation, temperature, radiation dose and cabin CO₂. An interactive body map shows eight zones, from mind and sleep to bones, colored green, amber or red. Each zone explains what it does and how space affects it. A four-level attention ladder tells astronauts when to self-treat, when to alert the crew medical officer, and when to send a ready-made report to flight surgeons. Thirty-day trends and a projection of bone density and radiation dose to mission end make the effect of daily habits visible. Daily missions, XP and badges reward healthy routines.

Grounded in NASA Human Research Program hazards and CSA radiation data, Centinela runs offline in any browser and gives crews autonomy far from Earth.
